procedural_history.originating_court: Trial courts (sentenced the petitioners to death under section 302 of the Penal Code)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Sentences of death for the offence of murder under section 302 of the Penal Code.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Judgment and Order dated the 6th December, 1982 of the Allahabad High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 1357/82.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached via Special Leave Petitions, Appeals, and Review Petitions after the High Court's decision. Additionally, several Writ Petitions were filed directly in the Supreme Court under its Original Jurisdiction.

issue.issue_text: Whether the burden of proof in cases of hostile discrimination lies on the State to prove that no other persons are similarly situated and that the treatment is not hostile.

facts: The case involves a challenge under Article 14 of the Constitution, which guarantees equality before the law.
The petitioner alleges they are a victim of 'hostile discrimination,' meaning they have been singled out for unfavorable treatment compared to other persons who are similarly situated.
law: The court distinguishes the burden of proof for challenges under Article 14 (equality clause) from those under other articles, such as Article 19 (fundamental freedoms).
Under Article 14, the person who alleges a denial of equal treatment must establish the facts of their claim.
There is an initial presumption that a statute is constitutional, and the burden to rebut this presumption lies on the person challenging it.
application: The Court determined that whether other persons are similarly situated to the petitioner and whether the treatment is hostile are both questions of fact.
As a rule, the burden to establish the existence of facts rests on the party that asserts them—in this case, the petitioner.

The Court reasoned that casting the burden of proof on the State would be unfair, as it would require the State to prove a negative: that no other persons are similarly situated and that the treatment is not hostile.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that in cases of hostile discrimination under Article 14, the burden of proof lies on the petitioner to establish that there are other similarly situated persons and that they have been subjected to discriminatory treatment.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the burden of proof in cases of hostile discrimination lies on the State to prove that no other persons are similarly situated and that the treatment is not hostile.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner argued that it is not for them to prove a negative, i.e., that their case is not covered by any permissive clauses.

Once it is shown that a statute invades a right guaranteed by Article 21, the burden of proof shifts to the State to prove that the person has been deprived of their life or personal liberty according to a procedure established by law.
respondent_arguments: The burden of proof lies on the petitioners to show that the method prescribed by the law is constitutionally impermissible.

cases.case_name: Saghir Ahmed v. State of Uttar Pradesh
cases.principle: If a petitioner shows that an impugned law ex facie (on the face of it) abridges or transgresses rights under Article 19(1), the burden of proof shifts to the State to show that the legislation falls within the permissible limits imposed by clauses (2) to (6) of Article 19.

cases.case_name: Khyerbari Tea Co. v. State of Assam & Ors.
cases.principle: If a petitioner shows that an impugned law ex facie (on the face of it) abridges or transgresses rights under Article 19(1), the burden of proof shifts to the State to show that the legislation falls within the permissible limits imposed by clauses (2) to (6) of Article 19.
Cited as a binding decision, along with Saghir Ahmed and Khyerbari Tea Co., on the principle of the burden of proof in cases involving Article 19.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a statute on its face violates a fundamental right, the general presumption of constitutionality is rebutted, and the burden of proof shifts to the State to demonstrate that the legislation falls within the purview of permissible constitutional restrictions. The person challenging the law does not bear the burden of proving that the law is unreasonable.
obiter: A judge reserved his opinion on whether, in all cases where a right guaranteed by Article 21 is invaded, the State has a further initial burden to prove that the procedure established by law is just, fair, and reasonable.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: When a law, on its face, is found to violate a fundamental right such as those under Article 19 or Article 21, the presumption of constitutionality is overcome. The burden of proof then shifts to the State to demonstrate that the restriction imposed by the law is reasonable, falls within the permissible constitutional exceptions, and is in the public interest. The court explicitly held that the burden does not lie on the petitioners to prove that the procedure prescribed by a law for taking a life is unjust, unfair, or unreasonable.
legal_tests_applied: The court distinguished the legal test for burden of proof in cases involving Article 14 from those involving Article 19 or 21. While challenges under Article 14 (equality) start with a presumption of constitutionality where the burden is on the challenger, this test cannot be mechanically applied to cases where a law prima facie violates a fundamental right under Article 19 or 21. In such cases, once a violation is shown, the onus shifts to the State to justify the law's reasonableness and constitutionality.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the legal position that the burden of proof lies on the petitioner in cases concerning the violation of fundamental rights under Article 19 or 21. It found that the judicial precedents supporting this view, which rely on a general presumption of constitutionality, improperly applied the standard from Article 14 cases to cases involving different fundamental rights. The court stated, 'To apply mechanically the decisions under Article 14 to case.s arising under Article 19 is to ignore the signifi~ant distinction between the nature of th,e rights conferred by the two articles and their purport and content.' The court also noted that a key case supporting this erroneous view, B. Banerjee, had overlooked binding decisions to the contrary.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the principle that once a petitioner demonstrates that a law on its face violates a fundamental right, the burden shifts to the State. The court reasoned that it is not for the citizen to prove a negative, i.e., that a restriction is unreasonable. Instead, the State, which imposes the restriction, must justify it. The court held: 'when the enactment on the face or"it is found to violate a fundamental right... it must be held to be invalid unless those who support the legislation can bring it withill the purview of the exception... it is surely not for the appellants to prove negatively that the legislation was not . reasonable and , was not conducive to the welfare of the community.' This principle was extended to the right to life under Article 21.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning is grounded in the policy of robustly protecting fundamental rights. Placing the burden on the State to justify a law that prima facie infringes on a fundamental right ensures that such rights are not easily curtailed. It prevents the State from relying on a simple presumption of constitutionality when a citizen's life or liberty is directly at stake, thereby reinforcing the judiciary's role as a guardian of these rights against legislative encroachment.
